newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. coffee official sees continuing tightness.
newsitem.headline: U.S. coffee official sees continuing tightness.

text.p: The head of the Specialty Coffee Association of America said he sees market prices continuing to hover near $2 per pound because of tight supplies that could last up to three years.
SCAA executive director Ted Lingle said the market had shown, in its recent correction, that it is unable to sustain a price above $2.00, however.

Based on current crop estimates from producer countries, and his belief that there are not enough arabicas and high grown milds to satisfy world demand, Lingle said: "You'd have to conclude that the industry will go through two or three years of fairly tight supply."
"I don't see it (supply side tightness) going away, particularly if New York C is under $2 dollars, which means these coffees are still very affordable," he said.

"If you look at the number of stocks available that are tenderable against the (New York) exchange, they're at record lows, and they're extremely low relative to the value of outstanding contracts," he added.
He said he sees spot prices staying just under $2 per pound, at least until the market gets a better read out on Brazilian production in the coming year.
"That's kind of the wildcard. Brazil historically has tended to under report their crop," Lingle said.
"They're definitely very conservative in their estimate for this coming year," Lingle said.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture has put Brazil's 1997/98 crop at 28 million bags against the Brazilian government's estimate of 22 million. Lingle said he had always been sceptical about USDA estimates, but he added that "they've always been the most accurate, based on what Brazil has actually shipped."
Though he sees solid support for prices of about $2 per pound, Lingle said the lesson from the recent correction in world market prices was loud and clear.
"The psychological message the market has sent is that it doesn't see sustaining a price above $2 dollars," he said. "That's what I think the run at $3 dollars was about."
Lingle said he supported the Association of Coffee Producing Countries in its call for clarification of the methodology used for its most recent coffee supply estimates.

But he said the job of drawing up such estimates could probably be better handled by a body like the International Coffee Organisation, since the USDA is "literally running out of the manpower and resources" to provide such estimates.

Lingle said the important thing, however, was that better estimates and a better understanding of how they are reached would give more transparency to a market where "virtually everyone agrees, whether you like high prices or low prices, that the worst scenario is volatility.
"It's not good for the farmer, it's not good for the retailer, and it's certainty not good for the consumer," he said.
